CITY MANAGER, CALE CURTIS, thanked the staff for their attendance at this afternoon’s City Commission Budget Workshop. He explained that last year, Margate engaged the services of the Gehring Group to perform a City-wide Compensation & Classification Study and that the Consultants, who were present, had concluded their report and had provided some recommended pay scales for consideration.
SENIOR DIRECTOR, HUMAN CAPITAL ADVISORY SERVICES OF THE GEHRING GROUP INC. (GGI) JOHN MULLER introduced himself and delivered a PowerPoint presentation where he provided a bullet point overview and described their methodology and approach. He explained that once all the information was collated, with the City’s input, GGI would then conduct a complete overall assessment of the City’s current plan and pay practices together with reviewing all of the job descriptions where this would be compared to 16 local municipalities based on percentiles. He advised that GGI analyzed that approximately 426 employees would need some sort of adjustment to place them into the new proposed pay plan which would cost approximately $500,000 to implement. He said that this would equate to a 1% increase with the inclusion of insurance, taxes and pension.
HUMAN RESOURCES (HR) AND RISK CONSULTANT, GGI, KRISTEN BIAZAR confirmed that if the City implemented all of their recommendations, the numbers did take into account the Federation of Public Employees (FPE), non-bargaining, Police and Fire Departments.
Discussion ensued including a question and answer session.
CITY MANAGER CURTIS explained that implementing this meant slotting the employees into a certain pay grade and City-wide, this would amount to $495,000 which would not account for future Cost of Living Adjustment (CoLA) and steps. He explained that the intent would be that the City would implement it first as the benchmarks were based on current year salaries and then CoLA and steps thereafter.
.
GGI MULLER explained that their recommendations were to adjust the pay grades and ranges, to present those proposed recommendations as needed to the collective bargaining and to apply the CoLA and steps in the next fiscal year.
Discussion ensued including a question and answer session with the City Commission.
CITY MANAGER CURTIS sought CONSENSUS to implement the pay grades for fiscal year 2025 and CoLA and steps going forward which would be part of the final budget that they would adopt in September. He explained that every employee would be part of the new pay grade and as implemented, it would be slotted into the next nearest step that they were at and would also affect employees that had topped-out for a number of years. He informed that the strategy for implementing this was fiscally responsible which was not over the top and it was important that every few years, the City reviewed their salaries and compensations and compare it with other municipalities in order to remain competitive and attract and retain good quality staff. He explained that this proposal would have to be negotiated with the respective collective bargaining groups.
COMMISSIONER, ANTHONY N. CAGGIANO, believed that the City always felt it was always important to ensure that the City was competitive and that it was less expensive to retain good employees then it was to hire new members of staff and have to train them. He confirmed that he had no problem with the proposal and thanked City Manager Curtis for looking into this.
VICE MAYOR, ANTONIO V. ARSERIO, had always been an advocate for their employees salaries and benefits and referenced paid maternity leave. He confirmed that he was in support of this and that a professional study was conducted.
CITY MANAGER CURTIS forewarned that the implementation was not going to put Margate at the top of those 16 municipalities but he wanted the City to be as competitive as possible whilst being fiscally responsible.
COMMISSIONER, JOANNE SIMONE thanked GGI for their study where she indicated that their research was thorough and that their findings appeared to be very fair for the City’s employees. She said that Margate had tremendous employees and that she was fully in support of this initiative and how the City Manager wanted to implement the same. She liked the City to be competitive and retain staff rather than leave due to the pay and had noted that they had been dedicated to Margate and had stayed all these years.
MAYOR, ARLENE R. SCHWARTZ advised that there was no change to starting salaries.
CITY MANAGER CURTIS summed up by saying that there was no formal action at this meeting but he heard CONSENSUS that the City Commission was:
- Supportive of the new pay grades; and
- Supportive of the implementation plan.
He confirmed that the next steps would be for the City to incorporate that into the next round of budget which would be presented in September and he would begin contacting the unions to negotiate the implementation for them as well.
title: COMPENSATION AND CLASSIFICATION STUDY

minutes_note:
CITY MANAGER CURTIS introduced the next Item as the FY2025-2026 Budget Workshop. He thanked Finance Director Diaz and Budget Manager Smith-Burke and expressed gratitude to all the staff who was involved in preparing the proposed Budget (PB) which he said was a huge team effort and explained the extent of the preparation that was involved.
FINANCE DIRECTOR, ISMAEL DIAZ, welcomed everyone to the FY2026 Budget presentation which he said took six months to put together. He thanked the staff and informed that they prepared the budget in the new Enterprise resource planning (ERP) system and announced that they would be going live in the next couple of months.
BUDGET MANAGER, DECIA A. SMITH-BURKE, welcomed everyone to the FY 2026 PB Workshop where she provided a PowerPoint presentation. She explained that the PB was a Policy Document, Operations Guide, Financial Plan and a Communications Device which she analogized to a Global Positioning System (GPS). She referenced a chart and said that the millage rate had been stable for the last couple of years with it remaining at 7.1171 since FY2020 while the debt services millages have been declining over the last few years. She said that the total proposed millage for FY2026 is 7.5389 which was a reduction of 0.278 at approximately $140,000. She advised that the taxable values and the operating millage rates were used to calculate the tax revenue and said that for FY2026, it included an increase of estimated revenue of 6.5% based Broward County Property Appraiser (BCPA) June 1st values. She advised that the City budgeted approximately $2,200,000 in additional ad valorem revenue and that the change in property values due to an increase in the payment to the Community Redevelopment Agency (CRA) of approximately $360,000 which means the net change in general fund budget was $1,800,000. She outlined the overall property values of Margate was lower than the average of Broward County and that over 7% of Margate residents paid no ad valorem revenue taxes and over 30% paid less than $500 for a year worth of services. She continued to go through the presentation by highlighting that Margate had one of the most reasonable tax burdens when averaging homesteaded single-family compared to other cities in BC. She also highlighted that Margate was in the lowest six when highlighting the Operating Revenue Per Capita Comparison and advised that the City did a lot with a lean budget and that they only made up 1/3 of the tax bill. She read through some of the budget items that were being deployed for the FY2026 PB year which included increasing funding in key areas such as public safety, infrastructure and trimming where needed. She informed that the FY2026 PB totaled $255,000,000 which was a 11.63 decrease from the current amended budget which was probably attributed to the City’s Department of Environmental and Engineering Services (DEES) Capital Improvement Fund. She said that the FY2026 General PB was $85,300,000 and she highlighted that the biggest proposed revenue adjustment was in the Other Sources/Fund Transfers category as a result of their projected fund balance and that the Fire and Police took the lion share of expenditures at 55%. She said that the ad valorem taxes were increasing by 6.49% pending July 1st update of numbers. She continued to highlight the General Fund and Improvement Program capita and Infrastructure projects. She summed up her FY2026 PB summary and repeated that the total millage rate would decrease 7.5389 as of June 2025 which was a reduction of .0278 and she asked for CONSENSUS to set the ceiling for the millage rate which was slightly lower than last year and advised that the rate could not increase.
MAYOR SCHWARTZ emphasized that this would be the seventh year in a row that the operating millage had not changed.
VICE MAYOR ARSERIO advised that legally, the City had to advertise it as an increase as they were not rollback but the reality was that the total millage collected from residents had decreased every year for the last seven years.
Discussion ensued.
COMMISSIONER CAGGIANO questioned Information Technology (IT) Director Garmon whether to the best of their ability, he had enough money in his budget to minimize against hackers. He said that it was also important that the City should ensure that the Wastewater treatment plant was going to be good for the next 40 years.
CITY MANAGER CURTIS said that IT Director Garmon did not have a microphone but believed that the City was covered in a way to mitigate their risks.
FINANCE DIRECTOR DIAZ confirmed to Mayor Schwartz that Margate had not increased the operating millage and commented that although the City would receive a DEES bond, it would not affect the millage rate.
COMMISSIONER TOMMY RUZZANO was curious as to where the figures derived from which were outlined in the FY2026 PB and referenced the average home sale price was $200,000.
MAYOR SCHWARTZ explained to Commissioner Ruzzano that the information derived from the BCPA and was not what it necessary sold for.
Discussion ensued.
COMMISSIONER RUZZANO expressed that the Finance Department and the Directors did an incredible job. He hoped that the pedestrian bridge project could be accomplished and referenced that the estimated cost was far more economical 13 years ago. He said that the City should contact the Broward County School Board (BCSB) to see if they could do a matching grant. He commented that he heard about the City Commission Chambers for years. He referenced four/five day work week as well as setting up a daycare for kids for Margate employees.
CITY MANAGER CURTIS explained that the City rebudgeted the City Commission Chambers and said that ideally through City Center Development, they will get some form of reconstruction of a City Hall, if not, they will look at doing some upgrades starting with audio and visual.
Discussion ensued including a four/five day work week and a hybrid work schedule.
BUDGET MANAGER SMITH-BURKE explained the next steps were:
- The City Commission sets the millage rate ceiling;
- The Budget Message and PB submitted to the City Commission by August 15th;
- 1st Public hearing on Wednesday, September 10, 2025; and
- 2nd Public hearing on Wednesday, September 17, 2025.
She thanked the City Commission for their time, attention and dedication and opened the floor to questions.
VICE MAYOR ARSERIO repeated that the overall millage was decreasing for the seventh year in a row. He advised that there were many Homeowners Associations (HOA) that charge more than taxes and that it demonstrated how well the City budgeted their money and the services that they provided. He questioned the City Manager how much flexibility there was in the budget if they wanted to increase an Item.
CITY MANAGER CURTIS explained to Vice Mayor Arserio that it was a difficult question to answer but the current budget had a $4,500,000 deficit which was normal for the City. He advised that typically at year end when their actuals came in, they would typically amend and beat their revenue projections resulting in the City being under on their expenses and over the last few years, Margate had been fortunate where they were putting money back into fund balance. He said that in the $4,500,000, that included the additional personnel for the Fire Department but did not include the implementation of the compensation and classification study which was a $500,000 plus steps so that they would be looking at additional funds on top of that amount. He thought that the City was still in a safe area where at year end, they would break even or close to putting money back in. He confirmed that the Community Redevelopment Agency (CRA) deal with BC was finalized.
VICE MAYOR ARSERIO referenced the completion of the downtown area and questioned whether the City could stop payments to the CRA or drastically reduce what they were contributing at this point.
CITY MANAGER CURTIS advised that by law, the City had to contribute a minimum of 50% towards the CRA and currently, they were paying 100%. He explained that the CRA had projects they budgeted for that would require dollars and they were flushed with cash that had been used in negotiations for a downtown development to get certain amenities as needed. He advised that as the CRA continued, there were projects that were in there that they wanted to finish off and not whittle down on the fund balance that it had and the projects included property improvement and commercial grants and land acquisition. He believed that the City would be very safe to start reduction and decrease to paying 80% which would freeze up approximately $1,500,000. He confirmed that this could not be effected immediately.
VICE MAYOR ARSERIO sought CONSENSUS to research reducing the Tax Increment Financing (TIF) contribution to around 80% based on the City Manager’s recommendation.
COMMISSIONER CAGGIANO confirmed that both the CRA Chair and Director have spoken about this and they have come to a 20% drop which was still durable to maintain a good CRA.
CITY MANAGER CURTIS confirmed that if there were no further questions on the CRA, he would take that as CONSENSUS on the City’s reduction to 80%.
Discussion ensued on the downtown and the CRA.
MAYOR SCHWARTZ polled the City Commission on whether the City should reduce its CRA contribution to 80%.
COMMISSIONER RUZZANO – Yes;
COMMISSIONER CAGGIANO – Yes;
COMMISSIONER SIMONE – Yes;
VICE MAYOR ARSERIO – Yes; and
MAYOR SCHWARTZ – Yes.
VICE MAYOR ARSERIO referenced home values in Broward County and Margate’s aesthetic property improvements and said that he would like to see the budget increased to $600,000 - $750,000 pertaining to median/landscape/curb appeal improvements.
MAYOR SCHWARTZ commented that it would be really nice to look at particular cities and make Margate look as nice as they did.
Discussion ensued.
CITY MANAGER CURTIS explained that the $500,000 was going to add a significant amount of tree canopy on Rock Island Road. He said that he would notate this for review and repeated that any changes that they make, they would incorporate into the budget amendment in November.
VICE MAYOR ARSERIO pointed out that their budget was less than 1% of the City’s budget.
COMMISSIONER CAGGIANO was a big fan of not touching the general fund but just wanted to ensure that there was enough money in the same to cover a major problem such as a hurricane. He repeated that he liked and was thrilled with what they did with the budget and said that the presentation was awesome. He reminisced when the Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) visited Margate last April.
MAYOR SCHWARTZ explained that the City Commission were having more in-depth conversations with individual departments pertaining to the budget and therefore, the meetings should not take as long as past Budget Workshops.
Discussion ensued.
COMMISSIONER SIMONE commented on the PowerPoint presentation and referenced that a 9% tax bill went to other entities such as the HCA Florida Northwest Hospital and also the Children's Services Council of Broward County (CSCBC) and asked what the latter entailed and whether it also incorporated the contributions made towards the Children’s Village as well as CSCBC.
CITY MANAGER CURTIS responded to Commissioner Simone’s questions and said that he believed that they were separate entities.
Discussion ensued.
COMMISSIONER SIMONE commented on the certificate frames increasing from $5,000 - $13,000 which she believed was an unnecessary expense and referenced that the children who received certificates for essay writing at the Memorial Day Ceremony were not presented in a frame. She also included the Students and Teachers of the Month commenting that some had received it more than once. She was not opposed to providing frames for a very special occasion but thought it was an unnecessary expense for everybody to receive framed certificates. She questioned what events pertaining to membership, league, conferences, promotional activity and travel entailed as they were significantly increasing.
CITY MANAGER CURTIS referenced the subscription memberships and league dues. He explained that the membership events were based annually from the various organizations and the conference costs associated with them were based on how they were annually and how many City Commissioners traveled to the same and he also explained how it changed when they did not used to do so much traveling.
Discussion ensued.
COMMISSIONER SIMONE explained that she had an issue with the Mayor’s Gala and asked that in the future, not to purchase tables of 10 and suggested that the City Commissioner who wanted to attend should utilize the revenue from their travel or office accounts. She expressed that annually, there was an issue as not all of the City Commission attended and were looking to find replacements to fill the table of 10.
MAYOR SCHWARTZ being advised that the reason why a table of 10 was purchased was due to the City being represented in one place at one time but she understood Commissioner Simone’s sentiments.
Discussion ensued.
VICE MAYOR ARSERIO concurred with Commissioner Simone’s comments pertaining to the big increase in the cost of the frames and suggested that discretion should be applied. He also commented on the Conference and fees. He indicated that it was a good job to everyone involved in the budget.
Discussion ensued on frames and Conferences.
MAYOR SCHWARTZ referenced Community Development Block Grant (CDBG) funds going from $200,000 - $950,000.
CITY MANAGER CURTIS referenced the Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) that went into CDBG and went via BC.
DEPUTY DIRECTOR OF FINANCE, JACQUELINE CHIN-KIDD, said that Mayor Schwartz may have been looking at budgets versus actuals and that it was some residual funds that carried over from year to year and that the City did not necessarily spend them.
Discussion ensued.
MAYOR SCHWARTZ referenced the Seminole contract and said that the City used to receive money from the Casino.
DEPUTY DIRECTOR OF FINANCE CHIN-KIDD advised that the City received approximately $140,000 this year from Seminole.
Discussion ensued.
MAYOR SCHWARTZ commented that the City should look for 100% of performance measures. She applauded the Finance Department for tightening their belts and decreasing the percentage to 39.38%. She questioned if the City perused for new health insurance quotes. She referenced HR pertaining to payroll professional services medical, page 37.
CITY MANAGER CURTIS advised that the City reviewed health insurance policies every other year and 2024 was the last time this was conducted. He said that it was the physicals that were performed for pre-employment pertaining to HR’s payroll professional services.
Discussion ensued.
MAYOR SCHWARTZ referenced Development Services (DS) and questioned a $300,000 increase and personnel. She was curious of the car leasing program was saving the City money.
CITY MANAGER CURTIS said that you would compare the actual budgets to the amended or PB which include the salary for a vacant Assistant Director position in DS. He said that it remained to be seen if the City would save money on the car leasing program. He explained that the City was entering their fifth year which was when they would start to swap them out which would indicate if they would receive a significant return on those vehicles when they sold them back.
Discussion ensued.
MAYOR SCHWARTZ praised IT. She questioned whether the CRA paid for any of the positions that were in Public Works (PW).
CITY MANAGER CURTIS did not believe that the CRA paid for any positions in PW. She referenced PW’s performance measures and commented on vehicle preventive maintenance performed on time.
FINANCE DIRECTOR DIAZ explained that those figures were included in the costs analysis.
Discussion ensued.
MAYOR SCHWARTZ sought explanation on the 6,550% increase on capital and referenced page 68.
CITY MANAGER CURTIS provided explanation via the PowerPoint slide.
Discussion ensued.
MAYOR SCHWARTZ referenced Parks and Recreation on page 75 and questioned if the increase in salary and wages was because the City was not taking the lease.
CITY MANAGER CURTIS advised that it was rebudgeted from the Administration budget to the Recreational budget.
Discussion ensued.
PARKS AND RECREATION DIRECTOR, MICHAEL A. JONES, did not have the specific page in front of him but did know that they were working with the Finance Department and HR as his department had many new positions that were not budgeted for last year that were added but not necessarily in the right division.
Discussion ensued.
MAYOR SCHWARTZ referenced page 77 under operating expenses.
CITY MANAGER CURTIS explained that the City was increasing their level of service on irrigation maintenance as well as median maintenance for that Item.
Discussion ensued.
CITY MANAGER CURTIS sought CONSENSUS on the PB on the maximum millage rate.
MAYOR SCHWARTZ polled the City Commission
COMMISSIONER RUZZANO – Yes;
COMMISSIONER CAGGIANO – Yes;
COMMISSIONER SIMONE – Yes;
VICE MAYOR ARSERIO – Yes; and
MAYOR SCHWARTZ – Yes.

CITY MANAGER, CALE CURTIS, explained that at the direction of the City Commission, for the last several months, he had been in contract negotiations and discussions pertaining to merging Margate Fire Dept with Broward Sheriff Fire Rescue (BSFR). He advised that there was a final contract price for the first year of transition, there were draft agreements and contracts in the back-up of the Agenda Item and today’s Workshop was also an opportunity to discuss this as a group and ask questions of the professionals that were here from BSFR and City staff.
Discussion ensued including whether to let the public speak.
REPRESENTATIVE OF 3080, INTERNATIONAL ASSOCIATION OF FIREFIGHTERS (IAFF) DISTRICT 14, MARGATE, ASSISTANT DISTRICT VICE PRESIDENT AND FIRE LIEUTENANT, BRIAN PALMER, thanked the City staff and the City Commission for taking the time to prepare for this Item. He discussed the potential of Margate’s fire service joining forces with BSFR which he expressed was near and dear to his heart and read a speech in support of the proposed merger.
COMMISSIONER TOMMY RUZZANO asked a number of questions to Fire Lieutenant Palmer. He emphasized that it was not the City Commission’s idea but the firefighters who requested it. He believed that the merge was a good move for both parties and that they would not be losing their Fire Department but it would be administratively operated under a different division. He said that recently, there was a fire where they had back up as there were no fire trucks available.
FIRE LIEUTENANT PALMER said that there was a great majority of his colleagues that wanted to merge with BSO. He gave a history lesson on the Margate Coconut Creek partnership and explained that when they separated, it left the City in a bad spot as far as sustainability of an organization. He said that it had also left Margate with 43 staff members and within the next three years, 23 were currently in the drop and that there were 24 employees with less than two years out of the 85 on shift. He said that when he applied to the City in 2017, there were approximately 300 – 400 qualified applicants that showed up on test day for 12 spots and most recently, they had approximately, a total of 30 applicants, some of which, were unqualified and very few that were competent to finish their testing process. He highlighted that the BSFR provided float trucks for a two-house fire in Margate.
Discussion ensued.
MAYOR ARLENE, R. SCHWARTZ expressed that one of her biggest concerns was something she read pertaining to the City of Deerfield Beach and she referenced a Sheriff addressing his people from a social media post. She said that it should be about service, costs and safety rather than a personal vendetta. She also queried whether the recruitment was down to money and benefits which resulted in departures.
FIRE LIEUTENANT PALMER said that although he was aware of the video, he explained that there were concerns within their organization where they may not be able to provide proper staffing, keep their units in service and provide a Fire Department to the public if they were to lose personnel to retirement, to retention and recruitment issues. He disagreed that it was strictly compensation as he said that a bigger organization was able to provide unique opportunities for the firefighters such as development of career progression, promotional opportunities and long term health situations which also affected the City’s recruitment. He advised that regional systems such as tri-counties and the bigger systems would traditionally have the best candidates in the pool but this was no longer the case for the smaller organizations.
VICE MAYOR ANTONIO V. ARSERIO highlighted that there was minimal career growth in Margate.
Discussion ensued.
FIRE CHIEF FOR BSFR, 2601 WEST BROWARD BLVD, TIMOTHY KEEFE provided a background on himself. He said that he had learned over 36 years that talks of mergers got framed as lost or gain but believed that it was about evolution and synergy and he spoke on those two keywords. He provided a PowerPoint presentation on the merger discussions between Margate and BSFR and praised City Manager Curtis. He listed the positives of the services of which a merger could provide which included move-ups, training and at various City events, they would be able to provide a variety of staffing. He also informed that the same operational staff would continue. He said that the total cost for Proposed costs for service which included three personnel on fire Rescue apparatus, Battalion Chief per operational shift, District Chief, Administrative Assistant and three fire prevention personnel was $22,464,349. He concluded his presentation by saying that the City had an outstanding Fire Department which he wanted to become a part of BSFR and hoped that Margate would see the long term benefits it could provide.
COMMISSIONER RUZZANO questioned Fire Chief Keefe what he thought would enhance the 911 system in the future. He said in the last few years, he had not heard any complaints about it. He also questioned why the contract was structured not to have any sets, limits or caps for the first two years.
BSFR FIRE CHIEF KEEFE explained that he was present as a County resident when they did the vote to consolidate dispatch and they took a 13 piece absent and combined them altogether. He advised that BSO was one of the largest systems in the USA handling more calls than most major metropolitan cities. He said that the 911 system had improved significantly, that Broward County had approximately 2,000,000 residents and advised that if it was a city, it would be the fifth largest in the US between Chicago, New York and Los Angeles. He explained that Margate was not an existing customer but there was a cap in the price which would not be exceeded. He said that he was working with City staff and that the cap was the implementation salary wise of the second year which was difficult to project.
Discussion ensued.
MAYOR SCHWARTZ questioned why they should go into any merger with the Sheriff when he was having issues with other cities. She expressed her concerns about the caps and said that if a situation changed or were not necessarily in the contract, the out clause could be “do it our way or go somewhere else.” She believed that it was about the money and indicated that it was difficult to increase salaries if the fire assessment fee had not increased over the last eight years and said that the City could not do both and come up with any agreement. She said that she was very proud of her Fire Department and spoke about Coconut Creek since the separation.
BSFR FIRE CHIEF KEEFE explained that one of the key advantages with BC and the BSO through the current system was that they have with agreements and that they were stuck to the four corners of that and he highlighted a situation with a small department during the Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic and said that despite having a number of employees being sick, they did not reduce service in one contract City, area or municipality. He said that they would have a leg-up in recruitment in the future as they consider this.
Discussion ensued.
COMMISSIONER ANTHONY N. CAGGIANO said that Pompano Beach had an 18% increase where their budget with BSO increased from $53,000,000 to $63,000,000. He indicated that there was a 14% projected increase of over $72,000,000 for 26. He voiced his concerns with the inflexibility on the caps and contracts.
BSFR FIRE CHIEF KEEFE was not familiar with the Department of Law Enforcement’s numbers but knew that the original figure that Commissioner Caggiano gave included the number of additional deputies which the City had requested hence the large increase.
VICE MAYOR ARSERIO advised that even though he did not like the tactic, he indicated that you could still continue to have discussions within the 90 days and made comment on the negotiations that took place with Coconut Creek. He informed that the budget increase was for raises which BSO would implement and if they did not merge with them, the City would have to compete with those salaries and that the price in the contract accounted for those earnings. He said that the information that the City Manager provided was that they could stay on their own and increase those salaries or go to BSO but the numbers would be the same and that the City would get through a merger.
Discussion ensued on contract negotiations and control.
COMMISSIONER JOANNE SIMONE had given this Item a lot of thought and explained that initially, she was against going with BSFR but they gave her some compelling reasons when she met with Brian and John and she had no reason to believe they were not being forthright with her with what they said. She supported the firefighters tremendously and believed that the City had the best in the County, if not in the State and that BSFR would be extremely lucky to obtain their staff. Her biggest concern was the contract being the 5% cap in year three and not knowing the cost for the first two years and said that once the City agreed, there was no turning back. She said that aside from the contract and what she had read from multiple cities that were not happy with BSFR gave her pause as they highlighted skyrocketing costs, lack of fiscal responsibility and accountability of BSO Tony’s administration. She explained and that the City would have no control over BSFR or the personnel assigned to protect Margate and highlighted that Cooper City complained that they have no input, oversight or control over the public safety operations or their finances. She alleged that in 2021, BSO received approximately $8,000,000 in undesignated contractual services surplus dollars collected from the cities for Police and Fire but they were not returned to the respective municipalities. She also highlighted the issues at Deerfield Beach and she was aware of other cities that were considering leave and forming their own Police force. She had reservations whether it would work with BSO Tony and said that she did not have confidence or faith in him that he would take care of Margate. She said that she was not comfortable in supporting this merger with BSO and that she would be standing firm on her decision. She hoped that there was some loyalty to their City for their veteran firefighters and that they would not leave Margate because of the money and said that the grass may not always greener on the other side.
BSFR FIRE CHIEF KEEFE responded to Commissioner Simone’s comment in terms of the costs and advised that it was thoroughly vetted and that it was contained in year one and there was no need for a cap when they were coming in as they were not in the existing municipality. He outlined that the only hiccup they currently had was to somehow capture that their increase in year two was with only the second half of the implementation and the study. He said he was the Subject Matter Expert (SME) that had handled and dealt with this and that the Department of Law Enforcement was not a part of this conversation as it did not need to be.
MAYOR SCHWARTZ read questions from the audience. She asked what the difference between BSO Police and BSO Fire Administration and if there were any separation of policies.
BSFR FIRE CHIEF KEEFE responded to the question.
Discussion ensued.
COMMISSIONER SIMONE read a document from the City Manager pertaining to a draft agreement with BSFR.
BSFR FIRE CHIEF KEEFE explained that the standard language was carried through every contract for years. He said that the number was the number at this point unless the City Commission wanted to add or reduce services which would be a conversation that they would have to review with the City Manager and come up with a new set of numbers.
Discussion ensued on the term “cap”, whether BSFR had three on an engine and Fire Rescue-Emergency Medical Services (EMS) truck and Fire Department budgets.
CITY MANAGER CURTIS said that regardless on whether the City stood alone or merged with BSO, they could expect anywhere from 6% - 9% increases everywhere. He forewarned that next year, if they merged with BSO, there would be a substantial increase but if they needed to stand on their own and bring up salaries and benefits to remain competitive, they were looking at some substantial increase as well.
Discussion ensued.
VICE MAYOR ARSERIO said that the numbers seemed to be apples to apples but questioned what the level of service and morale would be over the department that you want to have. He forewarned that if the merger did not go through, the City should have a plan b as a three station Fire Department was not going to work.
CITY MANAGER CURTIS informed that if the City Commission did not vote to merge with BSO, he would revert to the negotiating table with their union and hoped to come up with mutually agreeable terms that could keep them competitive in the market, offer the ability to recruit and retain staff and keep the Fire Department operational. He said at present, he would not have an answer for training and resources.
Discussion ensued on stories of buildings and whether the City’s equipment could handle it in terms of development.
MAYOR SCHWARTZ continued to ask questions that were written from the residents.
Discussion ensued on budgets and the fire assessment fee.
COMMISSIONER RUZZANO forewarned that the morale would be low if the merger did not occur and hoped for a plan b if one was not in place. He spoke about property taxes and values increasing in Margate over the last 10 years, that the City had a flush budget and informed Mayor Schwartz that they did not need to increase anything such as a fire assessment fee.
COMMISSIONER CAGGIANO discussed with many cities who paid more money to BSO then they received in property taxes but he said that money had gone as the City was spending the same. He indicated that the City Commission’s job was to plan for the future and alleged that the Florida State Governor, Ronald Dion DeSantis, was getting rid of property taxes.
FIRE LIEUTENANT, BRIAN PALMER, said that they were trying to give the City a tract to have a future to continue to provide services to the residents of Margate, regardless of costs. He said that the firefighters were very passionate and indicated that they were dedicated but historically, they were underpaid and under compensated. He expressed BSFR were offering an opportunity to provide a future for the residents at the same current costs as Margate. He understood the concerns about the caps and the future of the organization and he could not answer to his firefighters to stay at the City for loyalty as it was difficult to provide for their families. He said that he could earn more at Boca Raton and that it was not about money per se but also about opportunity, supporting their families, having additional trucks for back-filling, training, maintain their Range Safety Officer (RSO) Class 1 and being able to answer a call to the residents and provide the best service available. He was so passionate about this and did not want to see the City fall apart. He requested the City Commission to stand behind the firefighters.
COMMISSIONER CAGGIANO commented that they should not think that the City Commission did not care about their firefighters and said that Margate put a third man on, they built another fire station and that they organized medical testing. He said that the question was about the budget and deciding whether or not they were going to merge with BSO.
FIRE LIEUTENANT, BRIAN PALMER, apologized but explained that it was not his intention, if it came across, that the City Commission did not care. He spoke on the opportunity for safety within a structure and said that during the last 90 days, they have had over five major incidents from fires, to major accidents where additional support was required. He advised that BSFR allowed them to provide better staffing by backfilling in their time of need and that it was better for the residents. He explained that historically, firefighters died within seven years of retirement and that caring about them meant that you trusted their opinion.
Discussion ensued.
VICE MAYOR ARSERIO questioned the soft costs what the other departments had to go through versus managing a department on its own versus an external body. He sought Fire Chief Lorenzo’s position on the merger proposal. He questioned that if they did not merge with BSFR, whether the Fire Department would be sustainable as it was or was the recommendation to still merge with another city.
CITY MANAGER CURTIS responded to Vice Mayor Arserio’s comments and said that there was an external service number and a value they could put for that but it was not a dollar amount that would come off the budget.
FIRE CHIEF, ROBERTO LORENZO, said that there was a lot of passion in the room and detailed his backstory. He said that the Fire Department had overcome a number of challenges such as the COVID-19 pandemic, separation from Coconut Creek in September 2021 and the building of a fire station. He said that State Governor DeSantis was passing a law recommending a 42 work schedule which was also known as 24/72 instead of 48 hours and agencies such as Palm Beach County, Miramar, Boca Raton and smaller agencies had signed contracts to adhere to the recommended schedule. He said that the City was in a unique position and alluded to Fire Lieutenant Palmer’s comments that where they had 46 employees with 20+ years of service and that 23 of those individuals would be gone in three years or less and that the others would leave thereafter. He said that although the City was on the Florida Retirement System (FRS), so were all of the other agencies who were looking at a more competitive benefit and work schedule. He explained that it was discussed before that middle group of people that were going to take the department to the next level as more experienced individuals retire, they were in Coconut Creek. He indicated that it was a difficult decision to make but his recommendation was to merge with BSFR. He loved what he did but foresaw some challenges on the horizon and in his capacity as the Fire Chief and that he had to have alternative plans. He indicated that if the merge with BSFR did not take place, there were different things as an agency if needed to execute some of those items that were discussed. He indicated that it would be a good start if the City’s employees had an identical compensation but it would not satisfy everything such as promotional opportunities where some staff members may elect to leave and advised that there would also be challenges for the middle group.
Discussion ensued.
LOCAL 3080, FIRE CAPTAIN, KEVIN DELACOVA, advised the City approximately five years ago of what the right decision would be and said that it only made sense to do this. He indicated that there were other cities also looking into this or had asked for bids as he believed that the municipalities realized that the sustainability and the fiscal responsibility to do something. He referenced Palm Beach County in the North and Dade County in the South and said there was a reason why they were predominantly run by one department. He indicated that applicants were not attracted by smaller cities and that they had already seen it with their most recent hires as Margate received very minimal candidates which would continue. He informed that the tri-state counties were hiring in mass to cover a new shift that had been recommended on a bill for 24/72 and also offer higher better career paths, promotional aspects and any specialty units that they do. He appreciated everything that the City had done for the Fire Department up until this point and reiterated that this was the right move both for the residents and for the firefighters and he implored that Margate should not put this on the backburner again.
MAYOR SCHWARTZ questioned why Tamarac, North Lauderdale, Coconut Creek, Coral Springs or Parkland had not come up with the idea of merging with BSFR.
LOCAL 3080, FIRE CAPTAIN, KEVIN DELACOVA, alleged that one of the cities that Mayor Schwartz listed asked for a bid recently but advised that Margate should be proactive on this. He believed that there were other cities that could be watching to wait and see and if Margate merged with the BSFR, they would see other municipalities looking to do the same. He referenced Coconut Creek as a perfect example of paying more money for positions that were already been provided for. He informed that having a private pension could factor into a merger of this nature. He concluded his comments by recommending that the City should place this Item on the Agenda for August 20th, 2025 and make a decision.
Discussion ensued.
COMMISSIONER SIMONE referenced the words “the right decision” but forewarned that it may not be the right decision for Margate’s residents who she had a responsibility for. She also did not hear much in the way how merging with BSFR would benefit residents and also referenced skyrocketing costs. She also voiced her concerns about putting her trust in working with a sheriff who ran both the Police and Fire Departments that the City felt that they could not trust. She believed that the best decision was for the City to stay as they were. She hoped that the new development would provide more benefits for the City’s firefighters.
Discussion ensued.
VICE MAYOR ARSERIO highlighted the importance of mutual aids and advised that if there was a major call, he believed that with BSO, they would have trucks sitting in the station ready to go. He also believed that loyalty had disappeared where employees would stay in a job for 20 – 30 years and that the fastest way to get a promotion was to switch jobs.
Discussion ensued.
Meeting went into Recess.
Meeting Reconvened.
MAYOR SCHWARTZ questioned whether Margate’s Fire Rescue’s call out charges for residents would change under BSFR.
CITY MANAGER CURTIS confirmed that currently, the billing procedure would not change.
Discussion ensued on the services costing for residents, BSO Tony and the date of when this Item will be placed on a City Commission meeting Agenda.

VICE MAYOR ARSERIO indicated that from the calculations, they would only account for about 15% of that area as green space which could be due to contamination and that it was not open or accessible to the public.
Discussion ensued on cleaning the soil of the golf course.
RICHARD ZUCCHINI, LAKEWOOD ON THE GREEN, discussed maintenance to the golf course and referenced toxins and pesticides.
MARGATE RESIDENT, MINDY LEE, questioned if Vice Mayor Arserio was in violation pertaining to his comments on the golf course.
VICE MAYOR ARSERIO responded to Ms. Lee’s question and explained that it was not a conflict of interest.

TAMARAC RESIDENT, KENDRICK D. NOBLES, spoke about a misunderstanding and miscommunications about a business he proposed to have in Margate and explained that it was a transitional living facility for those who have spinal cord injuries and traumatic brain injuries. He asked what they could do to move forward and requested a meeting to discuss this matter further.
CITY MANAGER CURTIS, explained that the building official had provided clear instructions on what needed to be performed.
Discussion ensued.
MYRIAM JIMINEZ, 603 MELALEUCA DRIVE, strongly believed that there was a misunderstanding of what the City wanted them to downgrade of what they had for a transitional living facility. She requested a meeting.
VICE MAYOR ARSERIO said that she had his CONSENSUS for a meeting.

He referred to the Golf Club where he indicated that the houses were built densely to accommodate their Comp plan and be used as a useable space. He said that if they built on that area, it would require approval by an engineer that it was mitigated correctly. He said that schools have returned and forewarned people to be careful and referenced cameras. He discussed the garbage issue at Deerfield Beach and Coconut Creek and referenced a 2016 lawsuit that the City fought and won. He congratulated Ms. Sanchez who had served as President in her Homeowners Association (HOA) community.
COMMISSIONER, ANTHONY N. CAGGIANO, advised on hurricane preparedness and thanked everyone in the City for making National Night Out a huge success.
VICE MAYOR ARSERIO referenced the City of Deerfield Beach and understood that they were going to sign with Broward County Sheriff (BSO) and that the contract price decreased.
COMMISSIONER RUZZANO referenced a meeting and that the theory was that the City did not want to go to BSO because their rates upticked but indicated that the City’s rates had increased to 8%/9%. He was informed that in the first few years, the City would save money if they joined BSO and forewarned of the issues facing the Fire Department.
VICE MAYOR ARSERIO discussed Broward Sheriff’s Fire Rescue (BSFR) and said that although he was a big fan of increasing the salaries to match those of its surrounding competitors, he did not believe it was the overall solution to the department and would like to see a third independent study performed to assess whether the City required another firehouse. He advised City Manager Curtis that Margate should have a plan b if they did not merge with BSFR. He wanted the City to be competitive and that they were providing the best services possible to their residents.
MAYOR, ARLENE R. SCHWARTZ, apologized for not attending the City Commission meeting in person.

minutes_note:
MARGATE RESIDENT, DONNA L. FELLOWS, thanked City Manager, Curtis, pertaining to sandbags and referenced Hurricane preparedness for the City. She also thanked the Police and Fire Departments as well as Broward County Sheriff (BSO) Fire Rescue relating to an incident where a child was bitten. She asked City Manager Curtis if the fair was paid.

Discussion ensued on the fair.
MARGATE RESIDENT, TRACY VAN WINKLE, said that there was an issue in her neighborhood last Thursday pertaining to sewers and thanked the Department of Environmental and Engineering Services (DEES) for assisting in that matter. She advised that there was a problem with the Checkers Center Plaza. She asked Vice Mayor Arserio what he had learned on behalf of the residents in the convention in Orlando.
VICE MAYOR, ANTONIO V. ARSERIO, responded to Ms. Winkle’s query by saying that he had learned about integrating Artificial Intelligence (AI) to the City, was provided with an update on the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) and attended his policy board meeting and networking events.
Discussion ensued.
RICHARD ZUCCHINI, LAKEWOOD ON THE GREEN, disapproved of the back to back meetings. He referenced social media discussions about safety personnel, in particular, firefighters and their compensation package. He recommended that the City Commission needed to look into raising their salary and compensation programs to come close to Broward County. He also provided his suggestions on development within the City.
CAROLINA CLUB RESIDENT opposed the proposed development and expressed that it would be disruptive to everybody’s lifestyle and could forsee traffic issues and chemicals contained in the soil on the golf course.
MARGATE RESIDENT sought a copy of a traffic study and questioned when would the City be breaking ground for construction for the downtown on State Road 7.
VICE MAYOR ARSERIO responded to the Margate resident’s questions.
Discussion ensued.
title: PUBLIC DISCUSSION

minutes_note:
COMMISSIONER TOMMY RUZZANO hated the two months off as well as the double meetings. He advised Ms. Fellows that the Carnival was not paid but there were penalties in place. He informed Ms. Van Winkle that all the elected officials were invited to the event in Orlando and said that there were continuous classes throughout the day. He also said that it was a great networking event and referenced discussing the BSO contract with other cities. He truly agreed with the Carolina Club public speaker and other residents relating to the golf course. He asked City Manager Curtis pertaining to zoning changes on that site.
CITY MANAGER, CALE CURTIS, advised that it would go to Planning and Zoning in September and then the first public hearing for the City Commission would be in October.
COMMISSIONER RUZZANO indicated that the situation with the golf course could have been stopped five, six years ago if City Commissioners said they were against the rezoning.
VICE MAYOR ARSERIO would not give his opinion on the golf course but he encouraged the residents to attend the meetings and referenced that there could be a lake, a walking trail or open green spaces which were favorable with some locals. He would not make any decision until it was before him as things could change and forewarned that there was a lot of fake news circulating.
Discussion ensued about the golf course.
COMMISSIONER, JOANNE SIMONE, congratulated the employees for their Years of Service and dedication to the City which was greatly appreciated.
COMMISSIONER, ANTHONY N. CAGGIANO, advised on hurricane preparedness. He said that it was a great National Night Out and thanked everyone who had an input in organizing the same.
VICE MAYOR ARSERIO discussed the recent sandbag initiative and said that although it had nothing to do with the recent storm, he advised last year that the City should be more proactive. He explained that Margate was still negotiating on the firefighters’ pay and informed of a forthcoming Executive session. He wanted to go with Broward Sheriff’s Fire Rescue (BSFR) but said that it appeared that the City may go in a different direction. He believed that subject to negotiations, the firefighter’s pay would be matched to BSFR . He advised that near to the downtown, a Hometown Heroes Program was next on the horizon which would incorporate forty units and would be dedicated to first responders and teachers.
CITY MANAGER CURTIS, advised that subject to availability, the public could collect sandbags which were leftover.

COMMISSIONER, TOMMY RUZZANO, addressed the contribution made to the Pepe family. He was unaware that the Planning and Zoning (P&Z) meeting got cancelled. He highlighted this Saturday’s Movies in the Park at Margate’s Sports Complex. He recommended changing the allocated times slots for the sign parking bays bearing “15 minute only."
MAYOR SCHWARTZ explained the confusion pertaining to whom the donation was being made.
COMMISSIONER, ANTHONY N. CAGGIANO, forewarned about hurricane preparedness and commented on the band that featured at the last Sounds of Sundown concert.
COMMISSIONER, JOANNE SIMONE, congratulated and appreciated the City’s employees who were recognized at this evening’s meeting.
VICE MAYOR ARSERIO, apologized to Margate resident, Ms. Pepe and expressed that he would always support a request on the provision that it met the statutory obligation and the City’s criteria and continued to discuss the donation process. He also apologized for people who were present for the tabled P&Z meeting and said that he received a text on Wednesday notifying him of the same.
COMMISSIONER RUZZANO continued to discuss the P&Z meeting and indicated that the Chair could have allowed the public to speak regardless of its status.
CITY ATTORNEY, DAVID N. TOLCES, explained that the applicant made a request to continue the hearing and the letter was received on the morning of the aforementioned meeting. He advised that there was no legal way not to hold the meeting but the motion to continue the matter was made, seconded and voted upon and as it was a Quasi-Judicial matter, so the City needed to follow certain processes and procedures. He said that the P&Z meeting was set for October 7th, 2025.
Discussion ensued.
MAYOR SCHWARTZ attended today’s School Board of Broward County’s Mayor’s Round Table with City Manager Curtis and discussed the amazing things which Joe DiMaggio Children's Hospital did as well as the topic on redefining schools which she explained did not necessarily mean that they were going to close the same. She advised that the next meeting would be at Coral Springs’ High School where they would specifically discuss the schools in this area and expressed that it was important for the residents and the City to speak up for its schools.
VICE MAYOR ARSERIO had a personal meeting with Broward County Public Schools (BCPS) Board Member, Nora Rupert, as well as the Superintendent and his concern was that Margate did not have a high school. He was upset to learn via a newspaper that BCPS were considering closing schools and said that the majority of them were under enrolled and indicated that most of the City Commission was opposed to closing their Middle School. He felt a little reassured after his meeting and was advised that Margate was part of this redefining conversation as it did not quite meet the criteria to close down. He outlined his preferred alternative options if changes were made.
COMMISSIONER CAGGIANO believed that in a macro view, school closures was an attack on public education and explained that charter schools were destroying the public school system.

minutes_note:
CITY ATTORNEY TOLCES explained the instructions on this Item and said that it would not be approved at this meeting but would be presented for a Second Public hearing at the October 8th meeting.
GREENSPOON MARDER (GM), PARTNER, OF 200 EAST BROWARD BOULEVARD MATTHEW H. SCOTT, introduced himself and explained that he was representing the applicant, White Oak Development Group. He gave a brief presentation detailing an outline and overview of the background on the redevelopment of a seven acre site at Cocogate. He explained that the plans included to demolish the existing shopping center, that a mixed-use development was proposed which would have multi-family units and a retail space on the frontage along 441 with lots of landscaping. He indicated that some of the changes would give an attractive entry feature to the City. He explained the challenges to build on that site as it existed with a bank on the hard corner and also that it was on a built environment. He sought help to facilitate this project by approaching the City about doing a development agreement that would involve Margate providing some incentives to promote their ultimate vision. He said that they were proposing to make 21 of the overall sections in the project hero units and referenced the State of Florida’s Hometown Heroes program such as the first responders. He also highlighted that they proposed enhanced and larger than required open space such as the sidewalks and outdoor seating areas. He also discussed the features of the project such as a lift station which he indicated would fall under the City’s remit. He explained that his client would commit to paying the full connection charges at the time of the building permit for the sewer improvements which would also serve the surrounding properties. He advised that it was common to ask for an expedited approval for projects for Community Redevelopment Agencies (CRA) and he also requested that the powerlines be buried.
COMMISSIONER RUZZANO referenced the outparcels and questioned who owned the bank.
GM’S PARTNER, SCOTT, explained that the bank was separately owned which had nothing to do with his project and that when Tire Plus' lease expired, it was anticipated that it would be replaced with retail.
Discussion ensued on the length of the lease.
COMMISSIONER RUZZANO referenced Coconut Creek Parkway and that there were two entry ways into the plaza and questioned if one of them would be eliminated. He also asked about the lift station and questioned the total estimated costs for this project. He said that apart from the verbiage, he had no problem with the agreement.
GM’S PARTNER, SCOTT, said that they were relocating their entry point further west as they would not be allowed to remove the one located at Lester’s Diner as they had two driveways. He explained that the lift station was used by other areas in Margate and it would not just be for their project. He estimated the total cost of this project was approximately $90,000,000 and explained the connection charges.
Discussion ensued.
CITY MANAGER CURTIS, advised that the City was not being asked to waive or credit any of the connection charges for water and wastewater and that in the agreement, there was a calculated dollar amount for those connection charges which would be finalized once the applicant applied for permitting. He advised that they would reuse the language to make that apparent in the agreement for the second reading.
VICE MAYOR ARSERIO said it was a great project which he was very excited about and highlighted the previous problems that had occurred. He also believed that this project was the gateway to their downtown and that it was a very appropriate area for this development which needed to happen. He gave credit to Commissioner Ruzzano and said that he may have recommended using the Hometown Heroes Program. He explained that this was not a live-local project.
GM’S PARTNER SCOTT informed that the law allowed the developer not to pay property taxes on any of the affordable units.
Discussion ensued.
COMMISSIONER CAGGIANO was looking forward to this project and said that it was part of the gateway to their downtown.
GM’S PARTNER, SCOTT, explained that subject to shovels on the ground, he estimated a construction timeline of 18 months.
Discussion ensued on Tireplus.
LAURIE BROOKINS, NW 58TH AVENUE, informed that her address was located almost exactly one block due west of this project and read a statement pertaining to her concerns on the same.
MS. CULVER agreed with Margate resident, Ms. Brookins and suggested installing street bumps. She was also excited about the Hometown Heroes Program and referenced affordability for the first responders and teachers pertaining to properties.
VICE MAYOR ARSERIO was supportive of the project and the downtown and advised that as there was going to be extensive development projects. He recommended that they review the surrounding neighborhoods by conducting a study pertaining to speed bumps.
Discussion ensued on speed bumps and conducting a traffic study.
CITY MANAGER CURTIS forewarned that residents were either for or against speed bumps and referenced seeking CONSENSUS from the neighborhood.
Discussion ensued.
title: CONSIDERATION OF A DEVELOPMENT AGREEMENT FOR THE COCOGATE DEVELOPMENT

VICE MAYOR ARSERIO initiated this discussion due to the current political climate and changes to the gun laws. He favored the Second Amendment but voiced his concerns with open carry. He explained that the law excluded any type of carrying of weapons in a meeting of elected bodies for City business. He believed that at City meetings, there should be some form of security upon entry of the Commission Chambers for City board meetings with a metal detecting wand.
CITY MANAGER CURTIS explained that if it was the wish of the City Commission, he would work with the Police Department and the City Attorney to return with a few different levels of security measures and the cost associated with the same.
COMMISSIONER CAGGIANO definitely wanted to move forward with this safety initiative even if it was a metal detector at the front when they had meetings. He indicated that the public would probably feel safer with some sort of security measure.
COMMISSIONER RUZZANO gave a history on why the City Chambers were locked and referenced a member of the public that used to send letters to the City Commission. He said that the Police did an outstanding job but questioned whether the metal detectors would be effective and referenced whether it would be a deterrent for others from the family feel in the City.
Discussion ensued
CITY ATTORNEY TOLCES echoed City Manager Curtis’ comments that they would work together with the Chief of Police to devise a policy for the City Commission to review.

COMMISSIONER, TOMMY RUZZANO, provided an update of yesterday’s Planning and Zoning (P&Z) meeting pertaining to the golf course which he said passed 2-1. He said that Broward County was becoming unaffordable and referenced that Broward County Public Schools were closing down schools and asked if the residents were going to get a break. He said that the City did a good job, had not raised their taxes in approximately seven years and commented that only one third of their revenue went back to Margate. He discussed the downtown and was concerned on the developer’s proposal to build 300+ apartments which he believed was almost identical to a previous plan eight years ago. He disagreed with the proposed destruction of Ace Plaza to build housing. He suggested that a policy should be devised where future cancelled meetings should be clearly displayed.
CITY ATTORNEY, DAVID N. TOLCES, discussed the postponement of the previous P&Z meeting.
Discussion ensued.
COMMISSIONER, JOANNE SIMONE, congratulated City Clerk Office’s Viveros' promotion to an Assistant City Clerk. She also congratulated the City’s Advance Life Support (ALS) team for their participation in Croatia. She recommended at yesterday’s Community Redevelopment Agency (CRA) meeting, a travel policy such as a standard room rate and car rental for City Commissioners who attend events such as conferences and that extra costs such as an upgrade should be deducted from the board members’ personal money. She deferred to the City Manager.
COMMISSIONER RUZZANO questioned if the City paid for room upgrades.
CITY MANAGER, CALE CURTIS, was not aware of that policy.
COMMISSIONER RUZZANO discussed Commissioner Simone’s suggestion pertaining to travel for the City Commission and did not believe it was required.
COMMISSIONER SIMONE disagreed with Commissioner Ruzzano and explained that it was being fiscally responsible to the taxpayers and she did not see an issue with putting together such a policy and referenced checks undertaken by the Department of Justice (DOJ). She also referenced the budget and thought she had CONSENSUS to reduce the distribution of the plaques which could be saved for special occasions and thought that Margate was the only City that presented them in wood frames which increased costs.
CITY MANAGER CURTIS sought the board’s direction.
VICE MAYOR ARSERIO advised that the City Commission could be polled now.
COMMISSIONER RUZZANO thought it was a horrible idea.
COMMISSIONER SIMONE wanted to do away with the plaques.
COMMISSIONER ANTHONY N. CAGGIANO, agreed with paper certificates for adults but not for the children.
VICE MAYOR ARSERIO liked the plaques and was in support of retaining the current format. He also liked the idea of trying to find some sponsorships to offset the costs and also discussed the City Commission’s $2,000 to distribute to charities of their choice.
Discussion ensued on the City Commission’s donation funds and the plaques.
COMMISSIONER CAGGIANO expressed gratitude for recognizing their fire team in Croatia and for the amazing job that they did and he discussed the same. He advised on hurricane preparedness.
VICE MAYOR ARSERIO thought Margate was a beautiful City which was run by amazing staff and discussed negative comments that were made at the City Commission meetings. He addressed Mr. Kraljic’s comments pertaining to the double City Commission meetings and suggested revising the schedule to allow more time between the two.

minutes_note:
COMMISSIONER RUZZANO was against the banning of social media comments on the City’s website and said that they should allow the residents to respond and that he believed that it was against the First Amendment. He asked whether there was any form of technology that could remove offensive verbiage. He commented that if the City shut down the public’s comments, the social media’s page would be less effective.
CITY ATTORNEY TOLCES replied to Commissioner Ruzzano’s comments and advised that due to the First Amendment, you could not censor the verbiage being published and highlighted the importance of consistency as that would not violate freedom of speech. He advised that the City was not regulating based upon the comments but it was on the cost expense that was taken away from City staff in having to monitor this.
CITY MANAGER CURTIS advised that Margate would be in the minority of cities that did not allow comments.
Discussion ensued.
MAYOR SCHWARTZ said that the pages should be for education and for celebratory things.
COMMISSIONER SIMONE believed that the page was for informational purposes only and did not think it was necessary to have any comments or whether they liked or disliked the posts.
VICE MAYOR ARSERIO said it was a tough one as the public should be able to compliment or criticize the City Commission. He did not mind constructive criticism as long as it was done respectively.
Discussion ensued including how other cities monitored their social media pages.
CITY MANAGER CURTIS said that as far as he was aware, any City’s policy could provide some level of screening of those comments meaning that it needed to be on topic and he could not have profane language. He wanted to remind the City Commission of why he instructed to disable comments from their Facebook page but did not want the staff to endure criticism via that forum and referenced an incident that took place with a YouTuber filming Margate Police officers.
Discussion ensued.
MS. FELLOWS explained that it was a shame that the City was shutting down public comments on their social media page and agreed with Commissioner Ruzzano.
MR. OJAR agreed with Commissioner Ruzzano and referenced engagement in any social media platform.
MS. VAN WINKLE referenced that the share button and anonymous functions could be removed from the Facebook page. She also commented on her visit to the Building Department.
MR. KRALJIC responded to Commissioner Ruzzano’s questions and read a statement pertaining to the City’s social media accounts.
MS. BERACHA stated that Margate residents were not able to comment on other municipalities’ websites about the City.
MR. ZUCCHINI said that the City’s posting was not a social media interactive page. He believed that it was meant to provide announcements and said that it was not a violation of the First Amendment.
MRS. RUZZANO appeared to be on the fence on this Item but suggested that if the Item was shared from the City’s website onto the viewer’s personal page, then comments implemented. She commented that she would like to see Zoom continue as she had experienced problems with Channel 78 on their live feed.
COMMISSIONER RUZZANO compared Facebook comments with Zoom and referenced anonymous participants. He suggested that they put the Facebook comments back on after the six months trial had ended.
Discussion ensued.
CITY MANAGER CURTIS required instructions from the City Commission as to whether the Margate was resuming social media comments.
MAYOR SCHWARTZ polled the City Commission as to whether to resume with the comments after six months.
Commissioner Ruzzano – Yes
Commissioner Caggiano – No
Commissioner Simmone – No
Vice Mayor Arserio – Yes
Mayor Schwartz – No
CITY ATTORNEY TOLCES confirmed that based upon the City Commission poll, the direction was for the comments to remain off.
title: DISCUSSION AND POSSIBLE ACTION - SOCIAL MEDIA COMMENTS

COMMISSIONER SIMONE conversed with Mr. Scott and City Manager Curtis.
COMMISSIONER RUZZANO conversed with staff today and had other brief conversations.
VICE MAYOR CAGGIANO had conversations on this Item.
MAYOR ARSERIO discussed this Item with staff and the representative’s attorney, Matt Scott.
CITY ATTORNEY, DAVID N. TOLCES, provided further instructions to the City Commission.
CITY CLERK JOHNSON swore in participants who were going to testify.
MAYOR ARSERIO called for the Attorney, Matt Scott.
GREENSPOON MARDER (GM), PARTNER, MATTHEW H. SCOTT, 200 E. BROWARD BLVD., represented applicant, Margate Acquisitions and explained that they were present due to variances on a multi-family conversation of the property known as Waterside Landing. He walked through his PowerPoint presentation illustrating the property location and said that it was situated behind the Community Redevelopment Agency’s (CRA) future downtown. He advised that this facility operated to be an Assisted Living Facility (ALF) and his client bought it a few years ago and invested millions of dollars in improvements. He said that the ALF had to be closed and they were trying to pursue converting it to a multi-family community of market rate apartments and as there was insufficient space for the conversion, it would not be able to meet the City’s code on parking. He said that they met with staff to see how they could possibly fit in much parking as possible which was difficult due to the existing site constraints. He explained that if this variance was approved, his client would then proceed to a site plan and special exception applications. He outlined that if this variance was approved, this would not be the end of this project as they would have to go through exhausted site planning and an special exception process where the City staff would review it and they would have to demonstrate how they would drastically improve the property so that they could revert to the City Commission to hopefully receive an approval of that special exception and highlighted that it could affect current landscaping. He also explained that this site was also effectively invested for 110 units and the specific variances and referenced parking requirements of 230 spaces and hiring a traffic engineer. He repeated that they were requesting approval of these variances and bring to Margate, a new, drastically upgraded multi-family community that would support the City’s downtown. He expressed his enthusiasm to work with Brookfield in creating a connection to the downtown either with a pedestrian or vehicular bridge so that the lake could be utilized to the public. He said that they would work with City staff on building a dock on the lakeside which could be accessible to the downtown. He also believed that this would drastically increase the value of this property and the associated property taxes.
A question and answer session ensued with the City Commission and Mr. Scott including assigned parking, renovating the lake and landscape and property taxes.
COMMISSIONER SCHWARTZ had concerns over this Item and suggested to remove one of the buildings to accommodate for parking and made reference to the Transit Oriented Corridor (TOC). She explained that this Item was a problem and continued to discuss why she could not support it.
GM PARTNER SCOTT explained to Commissioner Schwartz that they were not empty promises as if the variances were approved, nothing could happen until they proceeded with a special exception process that the City Commission must approve. He explained that the only way to have the property owner first proceed with the major reinvestment in beautifying this property and making it something that would be compatible and supportive of the City’s downtown, was whether there was some relief on the parking. He repeated that this was only the first step and categorically, the City Commission would get to review what they were proposing again and ensure that and they would prefer to proceed with this two-step approach. He also advised that reducing parking requirements was the trend across South Florida and nationwide.
Discussion ensued on parking.
CITY ATTORNEY TOLCES refocused the City Commission on the Quasi-Judicial hearing and advised that they had not heard from the City staff.
Discussion ensued
COMMISSIONER SIMONE advised that the parking in the City had been a major deterrent to many developers who wanted to do projects in Margate and referenced being the strictest in Broward County.
VICE MAYOR CAGGIANO discussed his own experience of moving to a development where he was assigned one parking spot. He indicated that when people moved in, they would have to adhere to the stipulation on the parking parameters.
Discussion ensued on parking.
DS SENIOR PLANNER, ANDREW PINNEY, provided a PowerPoint presentation and informed that they were appealing the decision from the Board of Adjustment of October 14th for Waterside Landing. He outlined the history of this site and previous applications that had been made and read the City’s code. He explained that although the application request was for 250 parking spaces, they determine a site plan that showed 268 and if the building was modified to 72 bedrooms and 35 three bedroom units, they could meet the parking requirements.
Discussion ensued on hardship and parking.
DS SENIOR PLANNER, PINNEY, continued with his PowerPoint presentation and advised that if they permit this move forward, he forewarned that there was a possibility that the insufficient parking could negatively impact the adjacent property to the north. He advised that the staff’s recommendation was for denial and on October 14th, the BoA voted 3-0 to deny the variance but the appeal would bring it to the City Commission meeting for their consideration.
Discussion ensued including the size of the lake on the property and the ownership of the entry sign off Coconut Creek Parkway.
COMMISSIONER RUZZANO did not like interfering with businesses, especially if it was a private entity. He could foresee the problems but thought it could be a great piece to their downtown as he did not want to see that property abandoned. He said that if the City Commission Board allowed him, he would be willing to negotiate with the applicant to acquire a 99 year lease with up to 300 feet of the canal and that they would develop it with parks with parking and a downtown.
COMMISSIONER SIMONE questioned DS Senior Planner, Pinney, what the purpose of the interior landscape island and of the landscape perimeter.
DS SENIOR PLANNER, PINNEY, informed Commissioner Simone that it was to beautify the City, provide shade and drainage opportunities. He described that it was every 10 spaces and one of the islands was required to break up the monotony and pavement of the parking lot.
Discussion ensued including on the aesthetics of property, green space, the variances and parking.
GM PARTNER SCOTT repeated that they were going to supply as much parking as possible but they were asking not to provide the interior landscape islands between parking rows. He explained that there were ample opportunities on the site for them to provide an abundance of landscaping to make up for where they were not providing it and that the goal was not to short change the City but to provide as many car parking spaces as they could.
CITY ATTORNEY TOLCES continued to provide guidance to the City Commission on this Item and said that there was no negotiation.
Discussion ensued including future negotiations on the site.
DS SENIOR, PLANNER PINNEY, clarified that the City Commission was inclined to grant the variance appeal and that the written application and narrative was requesting a minimum of 250 parking spaces but the applicants provided a site plan showing 268 which was a difference of 18 spots. He advised that depending on how the motion was worded, the City Commission could approve 250 or they could approve 268 which was basically a policy decision. He also asked the City Commission if they wanted the 2,900 square feet to be pavement with landscaping or whether they required it to be asphalted.
There was no Public Comment.
GM PARTNER SCOTT highlighted that the City’s Code speaks to a hardship of practical difficulty. He recapped that there were hardships with the site because it was landlocked by a lake and there was existing structures that were closed which provided difficulty on the conclusion for the full amount of parking. He thought that this met the criteria for a variance and more importantly, they wanted to clarify that they were not seeking to not provide any landscaping and that they would have to come forward with drastic improvements for this site for the next vote for the special exception.
CITY ATTORNEY TOLCES advised the City Commission on the next steps before voting on this Item.

COMMISSIONER RUZZANO explained that the City’s sports groups was increasing and thought it would be a great initiative that every child that signed up for their program, which was not exclusive to Margate residents, would receive a Calypso Cove pass. He did not believe there would be any real money attached to it but said it would attract more visitors to the site which he thought was a win/win and he looked at it as incoming revenue. MAYOR ARSERIO concurred with Commissioner Ruzzano’s comments. He indicated that it did not cost the City anything as it would be allowing the children access and the parents would pay for their admittance.
